seo.title: Teen Mental Health & Addiction Treatment | Plan Your Recovery
seo.description: Counseling for teens dealing with anxiety, depression, substance use, and adolescent pressures in St. Louis. Evidence-based, family-involved care.

hero.headline: Counseling for Teens
hero.intro: Adolescence concentrates risk. It's the peak period for the onset of anxiety, depression, and addiction — and the period when social pressure, academic demand, and the pull of screens and peers all compete with a still-developing capacity for judgment and self-regulation. Teen mental health problems and substance use are closely linked; treating one without the other usually fails. If you're worried about your teen, you probably have good reason. We help families figure out what's happening and what to do about it.

items.title: Anxiety and Depression
items.description: Anxiety and depression are the most common mental health concerns in teens, and they often look different than they do in adults. Adolescent depression frequently presents as irritability, risk-taking, or withdrawal — not sadness. Anxiety drives school avoidance, social withdrawal, and physical complaints. ADHD, often present since childhood, creates mounting difficulty as academic demands increase.

items.title: Substance Use
items.description: The adolescent brain is more sensitive to the rewarding effects of substances and less effective at regulating impulse and assessing risk. Vaping, cannabis, and alcohol are the most common concerns we see. Cannabis use during adolescence is associated with meaningful increases in anxiety, depression, and psychosis risk. Mental health problems and substance use reinforce each other — treating one without the other usually fails.

items.title: Screens and Social Media
items.description: Heavy social media use is associated with elevated rates of anxiety and depression in adolescents, with the strongest effects among girls. Problematic gaming is associated with social withdrawal, disrupted sleep, and academic disengagement. We address screen use as a legitimate clinical concern — understanding what need screens are meeting is essential to addressing them effectively.

items.title: Emerging and Serious Conditions
items.description: Adolescence is when more serious conditions — bipolar disorder, early psychosis, significant personality patterns — first emerge. Early identification and intervention matter. What looks like a phase sometimes isn't, and a clinical assessment can tell the difference.

items.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
items.description: CBT is the most evidence-supported treatment for adolescent anxiety and depression. It's direct and skill-focused — teens learn to identify distorted thinking patterns, test them against reality, and gradually face situations they've been avoiding.

items.title: Family Involvement
items.description: Teens exist in family systems, and treatment that ignores that rarely sticks. Parents are partners, not observers. We work with families to understand what's driving their teen's behavior, set consistent expectations, and avoid patterns that inadvertently reinforce the problem.

items.title: Building Motivation
items.description: Most teens don't arrive ready to change. We start by understanding what the teen actually wants and build a treatment rationale around those goals. Motivation is developed, not assumed.

items.title: Contingency Management
items.description: For adolescents with substance use problems, contingency management — systematic positive reinforcement of abstinence and recovery behaviors — has among the strongest evidence of any intervention. It's most effective when embedded in family and individual work.

faqs.question: What age range do you see for teen therapy?
faqs.answer: We work with teens from approximately age 13 through 18. College-age young adults (18–25) are often well served by our college student services, though we're flexible based on individual circumstances. Younger children have a somewhat different treatment approach and may be seen by therapists who specialize in child development.

faqs.question: My teen refuses to come to therapy. What should I do?
faqs.answer: Start with a consultation for yourself. Understanding what's driving your teen's resistance — and how to present therapy in terms that make sense to them, not just to you — can significantly change whether they engage. We work with parents directly, even before their teen walks in the door.

faqs.question: How involved will I be in my teen's treatment?
faqs.answer: Very involved, especially at the start. We meet with parents separately to understand the history and family context, share our clinical thinking, and work on how you respond to the behaviors that concern you. As treatment progresses, the balance shifts — teens need to develop their own relationship with their therapist. But you remain part of the picture throughout.

faqs.question: How do we know whether this is a phase or something that needs treatment?
faqs.answer: Duration, severity, and functional impairment are the key indicators. If symptoms have persisted for more than a few weeks, are affecting school, relationships, or sleep, or have led to behaviors that worry you, a clinical assessment is warranted. You don't need certainty to make the call — that's what the assessment is for.

faqs.question: What will my teen share with the therapist that I won't hear about?
faqs.answer: Confidentiality applies to most of what teens say in session — that's intentional, and it's what allows teens to be honest with their therapist. The exceptions are serious safety concerns: risk of harm to themselves or others, or abuse. If something rises to that level, we'll tell your teen before we tell you. Outside of that, what's said in session stays in session.

faqs.question: Do you treat substance use in teens?
faqs.answer: Yes. Substance use in adolescence — including cannabis, alcohol, and other drugs — is within our scope. We use motivational interviewing, CBT, and contingency management approaches specifically designed to work with teens who may not see their use as a problem. Family involvement is usually a central part of teen substance use treatment.

faqs.question: My teen uses cannabis but says it helps with anxiety. Is that true?
faqs.answer: It can feel true in the short term — cannabis does reduce acute anxiety in some people. The problem is that regular use consistently worsens anxiety and depression over time and significantly increases risk of more serious mental health problems. We take this question seriously rather than dismissing it, and we help teens and families think through it honestly.

faqs.question: My teen has been to therapy before and says it didn't help. Why would this be different?
faqs.answer: Therapy is only as good as the fit and the approach. We'll be direct with your teen — not just reflect feelings back at them. If the approach we're using isn't working, we'll say so and try something else. Prior therapy that wasn't a good fit doesn't predict what happens here.

faqs.question: Should I take away my teen's phone?
faqs.answer: Maybe, but it depends. A complete removal often creates more conflict than it resolves and can eliminate legitimate social connection. A better question is usually: what is the phone displacing, and what need does it meet? We help families think through screen limits that are strategic rather than reactive.

faqs.question: Can my teen do therapy sessions online?
faqs.answer: Yes. Telehealth is available throughout Missouri. Some teens prefer it for the privacy and convenience; others do better in person. We'll figure out what works. In-person appointments are at our Saint Louis office; telehealth sessions can be done from home anywhere in Missouri.

faqs.question: Do you accept insurance for teen therapy?
faqs.answer: Our counseling services are out-of-network with insurance — we submit claims on your behalf as a courtesy, and many families receive partial reimbursement through their out-of-network mental health benefits. FSA and HSA funds can also be used. Psychiatric services — medication management, ADHD evaluation — are in-network with UnitedHealthcare, Blue Cross Blue Shield, and Cigna.
